interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is a point named by two numbers, how far along from the origin first and then how far up, so that swapping them lands somewhere else, when you drag a point and watch its (x, y) label change, plot and read points on a grid, and read a tank's level against time off axes with names and units.
interactive.title: Along, then up
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens on a square grid, 0 to 6 along the x-axis and 0 to 5 up the y-axis. A point you can drag shows its coordinates in a label beside it, with the numbers it sits on picked out on each axis and its route from the origin, along and then up. Later screens rename the axes as a tank's level in metres against time in hours. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it.
interactive.ignores: The tank readings are example values, chosen to sit on whole squares, not measured from a real tank. Every square is worth 1 on both axes, points sit only where gridlines cross, and only positive coordinates are used. Negative coordinates, scales where a square is worth more than 1, and reading between gridlines come in later lessons.

numbers.label: The grid runs 0 to 6 along the x-axis and 0 to 5 up the y-axis, each square a step of 1, in every step
(3, 2) is 3 steps along from the origin (0, 0), then 2 steps up, in step 2
The point glides from (2, 1) along to (5, 1), then up to (5, 4), and can be dragged to any crossing, in step 3
Plot (4, 1): 4 along, then 1 up; (1, 4) swaps the numbers, and (3, 0) counts from the origin as if it were (1, 1), in step 4
The marked point is (2, 4), not (4, 2) (swapped) or (3, 5) (the gridlines counted, the axis as 1), in step 5
(4, 1) and (1, 4): the same two numbers, swapped, land on different points, in step 6
(2, 3) is point B; A is (3, 2), swapped, and C is (1, 2), counted from 1, in step 7
Example tank readings: time 0 to 6 h along, level 0 to 5 m up; (2, 3) is 3 m at 2 h, in step 8
The example reading (5, 2) says 5 h and 2 m, not 2 h and 5 m or 6 h and 3 m, in step 9
An example reading of 4 m at 3 h plots at (3, 4), not (4, 3) or (2, 3), in step 10
3 up and 5 along is written (5, 3), along first, not (3, 5), in step 11
A reading of (4, 2) plotted at (2, 4) has its numbers swapped, in step 12

explain.text:
A coordinate grid is built on two number lines at right angles, the [[x-axis]] running across and the [[y-axis]] running up. On this lesson's grids they sit along the bottom and up the side. They meet at 0 on both, a point called the [[origin]] and written (0, 0). Any other point is named by two numbers in brackets, its [[coordinates]]. The first says how far along from the origin and the second how far up. Coordinates are written alphabetically, so x comes before y,[^1] and Bitesize's way to remember the order is to go along the hallway before you go up the stairs.[^2] So (3, 2) means start at the origin, count 3 steps along, then 2 steps up. A step is the gap between two gridlines, so the origin itself is 0 along and 0 up, and the first line along is 1.

Swap two different numbers and you land somewhere else. (4, 1) is 4 along and 1 up, low and to the right, while (1, 4) is 1 along and 4 up, high and to the left. Oak National Academy notes that pupils might confuse the x-axis and y-axis and count along the wrong one,[^3] and suggests marking the axes clearly with arrows or labels.[^4] So count along the x-axis first, then up the y-axis. When a graph's axes carry names and units in place of x and y, the order is the same. With time in hours along the bottom and a tank's level in metres up the side, the point (2, 3) says the level was 3 m at 2 h, while (3, 2) would say 2 m at 3 h. So read the axis names before the numbers. This lesson uses only positive numbers and squares worth 1; negatives and other scales come later.

**A point is written (x, y), how far along from the origin and then how far up. Swapping two different numbers moves the point, so count along the x-axis first, and on a real graph read the axis names first.**

practice.text:
**Rule of thumb:** Start at the origin. Go along by the first number, then up by the second. Where each square is 1, count the steps between gridlines, not the lines themselves.

**Worked example:** Plot (4, 1). Start at (0, 0), count 4 steps along the x-axis, then 1 step up. The point sits low and to the right. Read back, it is 4 along and 1 up, so (4, 1). Going 4 up and 1 along instead lands on (1, 4).

**Common mistakes**
- Swapping the numbers. Pupils might confuse the x-axis and y-axis and count along the wrong one,[^3] so (4, 1) can end up plotted at (1, 4). Mark the axes clearly,[^4] then count along the x-axis first, then up.
- Reading a graph's point up first. With time in hours along and level in metres up, the point (5, 2) is 2 m at 5 h, not 5 m at 2 h, because x comes before y.[^1]
